analysis.one_liner: Makes hardrock mining companies pay a fee to clean up abandoned mines polluting land and water.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in committee for two years, never got a vote in either chamber, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge hardrock mining companies a fee of 2% to 5% of net proceeds from mines on patented federal claims, with smaller producers under $500,000 in annual sales exempt. The money would go into a Treasury fund used to seal old mine shafts, control erosion, and clean up water pollution from abandoned mines. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near abandoned hardrock mines — the bill funds sealing dangerous mine entries, treating acid mine drainage and water pollution, planting eroded land, and fixing ground subsidence [S3]. Taxpayers also gain, since cleanup costs that now fall on the public would be shifted onto the mining companies that profited from the claims [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Abandoned Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund paid for by a fee of 2% to 5% of net proceeds, scaled to how profitable each mine is, from companies producing hardrock minerals on patented mining claims.

Spends the fund on the cleanup ordinary people actually live near: sealing and grading abandoned mine entries, treating and controlling water pollution from abandoned mine drainage, replanting land to stop erosion and sedimentation, and repairing ground subsidence from old deep mines.
Exempts small producers with less than $500,000 in gross proceeds a year, so the fee falls on larger operations rather than family-scale miners.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies producing from patented claims under the 1872 general mining law, which currently pay no such fee. Because net proceeds are calculated after deducting extraction, transport, refining, and other costs [S3], the effective charge on gross revenue is smaller than the headline rates suggest.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on patented claims

drawbacks.text: The fee reaches only mines on patented claims; producers on unpatented claims and other hardrock operations pay nothing, leaving most of the cleanup bill for the old mine legacy to be covered by just part of the industry.
Sites already listed under Superfund or the Uranium Mill Tailings Radiation Control Act are excluded from the fund, so some of the worst abandoned mine sites would get no help from this money.
Fund spending is subject to congressional appropriations, so money collected from miners could sit unspent if Congress declines to appropriate it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cleanup purpose is real and popular — abandoned hardrock mines litter the West with poisoned water and open shafts, and taxpayers otherwise eat those costs. But the bill is narrow: it taxes only patented-claim producers, exempts the worst Superfund-listed sites, and leaves spending to the appropriations process. It is a modest, decently designed step rather than a full fix for the abandoned mine legacy.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, together with Rep. Nick Rahall of West Virginia.
The House referred it to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Resources Committee the same day.
Three weeks later it was sent to the Resources subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and the Interior Department was asked for its comments — the last recorded action.
Twenty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all Democrats and no Republicans, but no committee or floor vote ever took place during the two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: they never had to pay the reclamation fee, and the cost of cleaning up abandoned mines stayed where it was, on taxpayers and affected communities.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies, which avoided the fee

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee; it stalled after referral to the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill, which sat in his committee for the entire Congress.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed fee-based mining law reform proposals during this era, as it had throughout the 1990s mining law debates.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on or acted to move the bill.

industries.note: Producers on patented claims would pay 2% to 5% of net proceeds into the cleanup fund — money they currently keep, since the 1872 mining law lets them take minerals from public land without such payments. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against communities living with abandoned mine pollution.
Fund spending on sealing shafts, treating mine drainage, and revegetation would create paid reclamation work. Their gain tracks the public's interest in cleanup.
